The words

I heard the bells on Christmas day
Their old familiar carols play,
And wild and sweet the words repeat
Of peace on earth, good will to men.

And thought how, as the day had come,
The belfries of all Christendom
Had rolled along th'unbroken song
Of peace on earth, good will to men.

Till ringing, singing on its way
The world revolved from night to day,
A voice, a chime, a chant sublime
Of peace on earth, good will to men.

And in despair I bowed my head
"There is no peace on earth," I said,
"For hate is strong and mocks the song
Of peace on earth, good will to men."

Then pealed the bells more loud and deep:
"God is not dead, nor doth He sleep;
The wrong shall fail, the right prevail
With peace on earth, good will to men."

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum Eb and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (E♭), on the word “I”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic re fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

The words are by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, first published in 1864. The tune, WALTHAM (CALKIN), is by John Baptiste Calkin (1872). This version of the melody and the words comes from the Open Hymnal Project.

  • Words (1864): Henry Wadsworth Longfellow (1807–1882)
  • Music (1872): John Baptiste Calkin (1827–1905)

Questions about I Heard the Bells on Christmas Day

What is the doh of I Heard the Bells on Christmas Day?

In this version, in Eb major, doh is Eb. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does I Heard the Bells on Christmas Day start on?

It starts on d (E♭ in Eb major), a pickup on the word “I” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is I Heard the Bells on Christmas Day in the public domain?

Yes. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow died in 1882, John Baptiste Calkin died in 1905; the words were first published in 1864 and the music in 1872. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
